reason: These are shipped defaults chosen from benchmark runs, not a JavaScript mechanism. The Go default configuration should start from the same defaults and keep the guard as an optional component; the filesystem-tools area confirms the values.
summary: The `apply_patch` file-editing tool is on by default in the base profiles, and the read-before-write guard (the filesystem observation policy, which refuses a write to a file the model has not read or that changed since the read) ships switched off; a deployment turns it back on with one setting.

reason: One source of truth for what a share can grant closes the gap where a plugin's own declaration widened a viewer's reach. The rule is independent of the language: the Go host enumerates its own registered remote methods in place of the upstream Typert registry.
summary: The list of plugin methods a share may expose to a viewer is read from the host's live method registry instead of being declared by each plugin. A share stores only per-method policies, and the host intersects each policy with that list before a call is dispatched; core methods and LiveShare's own methods are never in the list.

reason: Keeping drafts on the code host removes a second store and makes drafts started elsewhere visible. It also suits a server-rendered UI, which has no browser-side store; the small remainder upstream keeps in the browser (review summary, publication records) needs a host-side home that the forge area must choose.
summary: A pull request comment the user keeps for later is stored in the user's pending review on the code host, not in the browser. The changes view shows pending comments with the host's threads, and every write re-checks the head commit and is never retried.

reason: The goal, one home for session facts that does not take width from the transcript, stands. Upstream reaches it with React slots and a gutter width published by the Chat View; the Go host renders the panel as an HTML fragment. A small script is still needed, because the note itself records that docked and overlay differ in behaviour (focus, Escape, outside press) and not only in size.
summary: Facts about the current session (project directory, change requests, outputs) are shown in one floating panel beside the transcript. The panel docks only while the gutter next to the transcript is wide enough; without room, the header button opens it as a temporary overlay.

reason: The import is host-side work on a documented export format and is in scope under DH-ADR-1. The upload dialog becomes a plain HTML form with a progress stream; the mapping rules from export to session events must be restated for the Go session format by the area that owns it.
summary: An experimental plugin imports the ZIP produced by the DeepSeek website's "export all chats" action. The host receives the upload, turns the most recent conversations into stored sessions in a chosen workspace one at a time, and streams progress; the user can then continue any of them.

reason: Declarative, pure rules keep recognition deterministic for replay and let a new code host be added without editing the shared package. Both properties are wanted in Go, where each provider is a compiled-in component that registers its rule.
summary: Each code-host provider registers a declarative rule that describes its command-line tool (`gh`, `glab`): which subcommands create or reference a change request and how to map a parsed command to a URL. The shared package keeps the tokenizer and the projection, and the projection's version is derived from the set of registered rules so that a checkpoint built under other rules is discarded.

reason: The feature and its host-side rules (optional provider capability, one search per list, reads by URL limited to callers allowed to use the host's code-host credentials) stand. The page itself is rendered by the Go host instead of being a React page.
summary: A Code review page lists the open change requests that ask for the user's review, that the user created, or that involve the user, and shows one of them in full without needing a session. The lists are read only while the page is open, and only the shown change request is polled.

reason: Two Go host processes on one home directory have the same problem, and the rules (no expiry, contention is a typed answer, a claim left by a dead process is reclaimed) are the ones the session write lease already uses.
summary: When two host processes start on the same home directory, exactly one claims the LiveShare owner state by writing a small claim file. The holder registers and changes shares; every other host can read them, and its attempts to change them get a typed refusal instead of silently stealing the relay registrations.

reason: A setting that takes effect immediately is easier to explain than one whose meaning depends on when a session was created. The Go design keeps the live read and, because it does not read upstream session logs (DH-ADR-2), does not need the retired session event upstream still declares.
summary: The list of models a subagent may be routed to is read from the live setting at each call, instead of being copied into each session when it is created. A change to the setting applies to the next call in every running, restored and child session.

reason: Expressing timing in CSS is exactly what a server-rendered UI with little JavaScript wants, and the technique does not depend on React. The Go sidebar can carry the same style rules.
summary: The sidebar scrollbar thumb stays visible for 500 ms after the pointer leaves and then fades over 200 ms. The delay and fade are a CSS transition on a registered custom property, not a JavaScript timer, and reduced-motion users get the hold followed by an instant switch.

reason: Continuous-integration (CI) practice of the upstream repository: it describes GitHub workflow topology and runner pools, not product behaviour.
summary: Pull requests run the parallel required checks; pushes to the main branch additionally run a slower serial run on standby runners as an independent reference, so a mistake in the parallel job inventory cannot hide skipped work.

reason: CI practice of the upstream repository: runner routing for its GitHub workflows.
summary: A runbook for moving required CI jobs from the hosted runner pools to an in-house pool by setting a repository variable, per platform, without a merge.

reason: The Go design needs a dependency policy too, but sets its own: the framework module uses the standard library only, and each third-party module in the harness module is justified, verified and licensed in a library specification (DH-ADR-5). Upstream's bar (net deletion, health, fit) is a useful checklist for those specifications.
summary: Replacing hand-written infrastructure with a well-maintained external package is a legitimate simplification when it truly shrinks what the project owns, the package is healthy, and it fits the contract at the boundary. Settled seams are not reopened by this policy.

reason: Upstream documentation process: it governs how upstream maintains its own decision notes and their translations.
summary: Implemented notes of low future value are moved to a frozen archive or deleted, so that only notes worth keeping current remain in the active set.

reason: Repository mechanics: Lefthook installation triggered by the npm `postinstall` step.
summary: Git hooks are installed per worktree, so installing dependencies in one worktree cannot rewrite the hooks used by another.

reason: The obligation to disclose third-party software applies to the Go binary as well. The mechanism changes: each Go module is recorded with its version and licence in a library row that the trace tool checks (DH-ADR-5), and a notices file can be generated from `go.mod` at release. The generator described here reads npm manifests and does not carry over.
summary: The third-party notices file is generated from the dependency manifests and lock files, and a test fails when the committed file is stale, so the licence disclosure cannot drift from the real dependencies.

reason: Review and merge practice of the upstream repository.
summary: Chains of dependent pull requests use GitHub's native stack object and are landed with the stack command; rebasing a reviewed branch is allowed.

reason: CI practice. The lesson for Go is only that Windows behaviour must be tested on real Windows, which the Go design states as real-environment scenarios in the areas concerned.
summary: Every pull request runs build, coverage and native tests on real Windows, because Wine on Linux cannot prove NTFS, access-control, pseudo-terminal or process behaviour; the Wine run stays as a post-merge check.

reason: Review practice: GitHub label policy of the upstream repository.
summary: Every pull request carries exactly one `kind/*` label and at least one `area/*` label from a fixed taxonomy.

reason: Review practice: issue-tracker automation of the upstream repository.
summary: Review webhooks are treated as commands that move an issue between "In review" and "In progress" on the project board.

reason: npm tooling: publication of npm packages. The Go design ships Go modules and binaries, and the two Go modules are versioned under DH-ADR-5.
summary: The product packages, the vendored cordis packages and the native packages are published to npm as three independent version sequences with separate workflows and tags.

reason: Upstream writing and naming policy enforced by a repository script. The Go documents follow their own plain-English rule to name the exact concept.
summary: One overloaded word for "origin" is banned from all maintained text and identifiers, and a check enforces it; each use must name the exact concept instead.

reason: npm tooling: the note exists because of npm peer-dependency resolution cost. A Go binary has no install-time dependency resolution.
summary: A package that has both a browser part and a host part declares its dependencies by which part uses them, so that installing the published command-line tool does not make npm resolve deep chains of peer dependencies.

reason: CI practice: runner selection for one upstream workflow.
summary: The Windows build of the Python SDK runtime always runs on GitHub-hosted Windows runners and no longer follows the failover switch to the in-house pool.

reason: CI practice: runner routing for the upstream GitHub workflows.
summary: A third-party runner provider can be selected as a CI failover target by a repository variable, never as the default.

reason: A macOS desktop release still has to be signed and notarized, so the goal stands. The steps described are specific to electron-builder; the desktop shell is a Go webview application (DH-ADR-3) with its own packaging, and the desktop area decides whether two parallel submissions are still worth the complexity.
summary: The macOS desktop release signs one application bundle, makes two isolated copies, and notarizes the update archive and the disk image in parallel, because stapling modifies the bundle and the two Apple submissions would otherwise run one after the other.

reason: The goal stands for any durable format: a change to what is written to disk must not land unnoticed. The mechanism is tied to the TypeScript compiler's type model. Inference: the Go design can reach it with a committed schema snapshot generated from the Go event types and compared in a test; the session area decides.
summary: The types of all persisted session events are normalized into one model with a digest per root type. A change to any nested type changes the digest, and the change must be acknowledged in a committed persistence-change record before it can merge.

reason: The rule stands: an experimental capability must not be part of the default product by accident. Upstream follows npm dependency edges and configuration files; with compiled-in components (DH-ADR-4) the Go check is that the default configuration enables no experimental component and that the default build does not import one.
summary: A check proves that nothing in the default product depends on, imports, or loads by configuration any experimental package; the bundles the launcher names as optional are the one declared exception.

reason: A reference generated from the real command tree is equally easy in Go and removes the same drift. The command-line area owns the generator.
summary: The command-line reference is generated by capturing the help text of the launcher, the plugin forwarder and every shipped profile, and following each listed subcommand, so it cannot omit a command or keep an old default.

reason: The goal stands: a user can switch on an official optional capability without finding and installing it by name. With compiled-in components (DH-ADR-4) the capability is already in the binary, so "shipped but off" becomes a component that the default configuration leaves disabled and the plugin page can enable; the npm runtime-dependency mechanics do not carry over.
summary: The installation ships a named list of optional bundles (official but experimental layers such as Agent Teams) that are switched off until the user turns them on in the plugin page; they can never be removed, and they are the one declared exception to the rule that the default product contains nothing experimental.

reason: Recording reader promises next to the persisted field is worth keeping for the Go session format, but the mechanism here is an extractor over TypeScript declarations and comment annotations. Inference: Go struct tags or a hand-written schema file can carry the same promises; the session area decides the form.
summary: The persistence schema inventory records, beside each affected property, the compatibility promise a reader makes for it (for example, that unknown kinds are preserved), so a reviewer can tell a declared promise from an assumption. Promises are declared in source annotations and must be established and tested by the runtime owner first.

reason: Upstream build process: a speed optimisation of upstream's Windows packaging pipeline for the third-party runtimes it re-signs on every build. It carries no product behaviour; a Go packaging pipeline can add a cache later if it re-signs the same files.
summary: Windows packaging caches the signed copies of unchanged bundled runtime files (Python, LibreOffice), keyed by content, certificate and signing tool, so that a build does not repeat hardware-token signing and timestamping for files that did not change.

reason: A Go Windows binary and installer are signed with the same tool, certificate and hardware token, so the failure analysis holds unchanged: a timestamp-server error must not cause a second use of the private key. The desktop and release area should keep the two-phase rule.
summary: Windows code signing is done in two separate phases: sign a private copy once with the hardware token and no timestamp, then add the timestamp without credentials, retrying only the timestamp at most three times. A hardware or verification failure keeps the interlock and is never recovered automatically.

reason: TypeScript tooling: the rule is about a TypeScript type-assertion form that has no Go counterpart.
summary: New type assertions through `unknown` are forbidden in first-party code; existing ones are held in a baseline that may only shrink.

reason: TypeScript tooling: a syntax checker for JavaScript `catch` clauses. Go has no exceptions; the matching Go habit (never discard an error without a stated reason) is a lint setting, not a design decision.
summary: An empty `catch` clause must name the error, say why discarding it is safe, and wrap a single statement; a checker with a shrinking baseline enforces the form.

reason: npm tooling: it measures npm's dependency resolution of the published packages.
summary: The check that installs two releases side by side with npm decides pass or fail by a work budget computed from the dependency graph, not by a wall-clock timeout that depends on the runner.

reason: TypeScript and CI tooling: scheduling of `tsc` programs in upstream's workflows.
summary: Pull-request jobs that only need compiled artifacts build them without re-running the repository-wide TypeScript checks for tests and scripts, which the required build jobs still run.

reason: The goal, no dormant component that ships without a stated role, stands, and Go's compiler does not catch a component that is registered but never configured. Inference: the Go check compares the registry of compiled-in components (DH-ADR-4) with the shipped configurations, instead of walking npm packages.
summary: Every non-experimental package must either be used by a shipped profile, a runtime import or an optional capability, or carry an explicit classification (optional integration, SDK, build tool, test tool and so on) that records its role. A check fails on a package that is neither.

reason: npm tooling: the content of published npm tarballs. A Go module is published as source by construction.
summary: Every published npm package includes its TypeScript source, source maps and declaration maps, and bundles are compressed without renaming identifiers, so a plugin author can read the implementation and a stack trace names the original code.

reason: The criterion (reader behaviour, not structural difference) is independent of the language and avoids a version bump and migration for every optional field. The Go session format should adopt it from its first release; "already released readers" then means released Go binaries.
summary: The session format version number changes only when existing readers would misread the new data. A change keeps the same version when older readers resume correctly, safely ignore an optional feature while preserving its records, or refuse a required feature before they execute, change or repair anything.

reason: TypeScript tooling: scheduling of `tsc` and the bundler. `go build` and `go vet` have no such split to manage.
summary: The build is split into a command that produces artifacts and a command that only type-checks the aggregate test and script programs; the full build runs both concurrently.

reason: TypeScript and npm tooling: all eight items concern `tsc`, pnpm symlinks or upstream's code generator.
summary: Eight changes that make a cold build faster without changing any output byte or diagnostic, such as declaring React type packages only at the root and making the remote-method generator parse package configuration lazily.

reason: Upstream development process: hook and check scheduling for its TypeScript toolchain.
summary: Eight changes that shorten local Git hooks, checks and test runs, such as generating declarations without bundling and capping the default number of local workers.

reason: npm tooling: `dependencies`, `devDependencies` and `peerDependencies` placement.
summary: Experimental packages follow the same rules as release packages for which npm dependency section a dependency belongs in; the group-wide exemption is removed.

reason: JavaScript tooling: module evaluation order is a JavaScript concern. A Go program always has an explicit `main`, so the checked rule has nothing to check; the readiness and exit-code conventions of each child process are restated by the area that owns that process.
summary: Package source may not use top-level `await`; a child-process entry uses an explicit `main()` that reports its own failure on stderr with a fixed exit code.

reason: Node tooling: the runtime floor of the JavaScript product. The Go counterpart is the `go` directive of each module, set by the toolchain decisions.
summary: The minimum supported Node.js version is 24.9, with CI jobs pinned to the minimum and to the newest major version.

reason: TypeScript tooling: placement of upstream's code-generation step in its build.
summary: Remote-method metadata is generated from source before packages are compiled, instead of during bundling, so the build does not need a second dependency graph to order it.

reason: Review practice: merge-gate automation of the upstream repository.
summary: The weighted-approval merge gate stays a commit status, and a separate check run written by a GitHub App shows "action required" while approvals are missing.

reason: The goal, a plugin whose public surface is its registration and its contracts and nothing else, stands. In Go it is reached by package layout: a compiled-in component (DH-ADR-4) exports its constructor, config type and interfaces, and keeps everything else unexported or under `internal/`, so the compiler enforces what upstream needs a checker for.
summary: A plugin's entry module may export only what the loader loads (name, dependencies, config schema, apply function, or the service class) plus the service contracts and error types other packages extend or throw. A checker enforces it for both plugin forms.

reason: The Go cordis port exposes the same accessor (`Context.Root()`), so the same shortcut is available to a Go component. The rule should hold from the first line of harness code, which means no baseline is needed; a test or lint over the harness module can enforce it.
summary: New code may not read the framework's root context. Reading a service through the root skips the declared-dependency check, a listener on the root skips scope filtering, and the root realm is not the caller's realm; each legitimate use has a declared replacement. Existing reads are held in a baseline that may only shrink.

reason: One identity for routing, event sourcing and persistence removes a mapping no production path needs. Nothing about it depends on JavaScript.
summary: A live agent and its session share one identifier. There is no separate agent id to translate; the configuration keeps a stable label, and a fresh start mints the identifier from the label plus a random part.

reason: Grouping by timing made behaviour depend on scheduling accidents. Go's goroutine scheduling would make timing-based batching even less predictable, so the explicit rule is the right one to keep.
summary: Each call to send a message creates its own queue item and, if it runs, its own turn. Two sends are never silently combined into one turn because they happened to be waiting at the same moment, and the second turn starts only after the first has ended and its durability checkpoint has settled.

reason: Keeping presentation out of an automation transport prevents a third user interface from growing beside the web UI and the terminal. The scope decision is independent of the language.
summary: The Agent Client Protocol (ACP) bridge is an automation transport only: sessions, one prompt at a time, model configuration, MCP mounting, committed updates, cancellation and one-shot permission requests. It no longer renders editor cards, pickers or other presentation.

reason: A turn identifier should mean one model-loop execution and nothing else. The Go session log can allow extension events between turns in the same way.
summary: A plugin that records a log-only event while no turn is running appends it directly to the session and, if it promised durability, flushes explicitly. No artificial turn is opened just to get a durability checkpoint.

reason: Making the zone explicit removed session headers, migrations and a confirmation protocol. The rule carries over; the server-rendered UI needs one line of script to put the browser's zone into the prompt form.
summary: The browser's time zone is sampled with every prompt and logged on that user message; it is never stored as session state. The schedule tool accepts only a time with an explicit offset or an explicit zone, and the model is told to ask the user when the zone is mixed or missing.

reason: One authoritative store halves every contract, recovery and migration test matrix. The Go design should keep "one first-party store behind one interface"; which physical format that store uses is free under DH-ADR-2. Note that the note says the SQLite provider is absent, while the pinned checkout still contains `packages/session/session-persistence-sqlite`; the session area must settle which is current.
summary: The project owns and tests one authoritative physical session store. The storage contract stays neutral so that someone else could implement another backend, but a second first-party backend is not maintained. The full-text search index and the key-value store are separate, rebuildable or unrelated data.

reason: Keeping the loader eager and making consumers own their completion checks is the simpler contract. One upstream reason no longer applies: the revert was partly to stay close to the pinned vendored sources, and the Go port is owned code. The loader area should therefore confirm this verdict and must describe what a half-applied reload looks like to an operator.
summary: The plugin loader applies a configuration change eagerly and does not roll back: a failed edit can leave a partly applied tree, failures are logged, and each application consumer (command-line start-up, directory chooser, preset mounting) checks for itself that what it mounted is ready. A transactional reload was built and then reverted.

reason: The Go design should likewise ship no E2B backend and keep the contracts remote-capable, which the SSH providers already require. The removal still holds in Go: the blocker was a missing control channel in the vendor SDK, not anything in JavaScript.
summary: The three providers that ran files, commands and terminals in an E2B cloud sandbox were removed. Remote execution stays an intended capability: the filesystem and subprocess contracts remain asynchronous and provider-neutral so that a remote backend can be added without changing tools.

reason: One owner for creation, cancellation, result and cleanup removes the separate paths that used to disagree. In Go the handle maps onto a value with a context for cancellation and a result that is delivered after cleanup.
summary: Every way of running a subagent goes through one entry point that returns a handle with the child's identity, a result that settles only after cleanup, and disposal of exactly that activation. Local providers only contribute preparation data; the subagent service owns agent creation and lifetime.

reason: npm tooling: the note is about `node_modules`, pnpm overrides and lock files inside a profile. A Go profile holds configuration only, because capabilities are compiled in or run as plugin processes.
summary: The desktop application no longer deletes or prunes packages in the profile's `node_modules` before starting the host; resolution order alone decides which copy of a package runs.

reason: The mixed form multiplied schema ordering, admission and test combinations without adding a capability. The rule is a configuration constraint and carries over unchanged.
summary: Each agent offers its tools to the model in exactly one form: either as native function schemas, or as a single `run_code` tool with a generated SDK (programmatic tool calling, PTC). Offering both at once is rejected in configuration.

reason: One place to compose an agent is easier to reason about than two. The Go design keeps preset-owned composition and the rule that an unknown configuration key is an error; it does not need the parsing upstream retains for child descriptors written by older releases (DH-ADR-2).
summary: A subagent's persona and tool set come from the Agent Preset it selects, not from separate persona and tool-filter settings on the subagent tool. The removed settings are rejected at load instead of being silently ignored.

reason: Deriving presentation from the text removes durable metadata that had to be kept in step across prompt, echo and queue. A server-rendered UI benefits directly: the Go renderer recognises the blockquote when it renders the message.
summary: A quoted passage in a user message is ordinary Markdown blockquote text. The UI recognises it by matching the text; no separate quote index is stored with the message, so a hand-typed quote and a quote made with the composer behave the same.

reason: A wait that ends without a message leaves the model with nothing to act on. The narrower rule also keeps team coordination out of ordinary subagent controls, and maps directly onto a Go channel or subscription on one inbox.
summary: The `wait_agent` tool ends only when a message arrives in its caller's own inbox (or on timeout or cancellation). Task-board edits and other agents' activity do not wake it; a caller who wants a team member to act sends an explicit message.

reason: The Go team projection should contain only tasks and mode from the start. The other half of the note, ignoring historical member and message records, has nothing to ignore in Go because upstream session logs are not read (DH-ADR-2).
summary: The team state derived from the session log holds only the task list and the saved mode. Older member and mailbox records are ignored instead of being replayed through retired validators that could fail the current task board.

reason: A placeholder hid invalid tool-update state, changed the cached request prefix and advertised a tool nothing could execute. Surfacing the provider error is the honest behaviour in any language.
summary: When every tool in a DeepSeek request is declared as deferred, the adapter sends the request unchanged and reports the provider's rejection. It no longer inserts a placeholder tool to make the request acceptable.

reason: Supporting one program language keeps one SDK generator, one set of naming rules and one test matrix. The Go design should also commit to a single language. Inference: TypeScript stays the natural choice because the model writes it, but the Go host then has to run it in a separate runtime process, which the PTC area must specify.
summary: Programmatic tool calling accepts programs in one language only, TypeScript. Python rendering, language dispatch and Python-specific naming restrictions were removed; the runtime service itself stays independent of tools.

reason: This is the same separation the Go design requires between local tests and real-environment scenarios, and the same rule that a skipped or unconfigured required scenario is not a pass. The practice is independent of the language.
summary: Tests against the real model API run in their own workflow, separate from the keyless checks that any fork can run. A missing credential is a loud failure, never a silent pass.

reason: Replaying recorded model output into the real host while a real browser drives the real page is the right keyless evidence for a server-rendered UI too. The recordings must be made in the Go session format (DH-ADR-2) and the snapshots re-taken for the new HTML, so nothing is reused except the method.
summary: The web UI has a deterministic browser test lane that needs no API key: recorded sessions are replayed as model output against the real assembled host, a real browser drives the page, and the visible states are compared with normalized accessibility-tree snapshots.

reason: The goal stands: a long reasoning stream must not cause one redraw per chunk. With HTML streamed over server-sent events (DH-ADR-3) the coalescing moves to the Go host, which should batch live updates to a bounded rate before sending them; the React publication mechanism does not exist.
summary: Every live chunk of a streaming reply is folded into state at once, but the UI is redrawn at most once per browser animation frame; the durable settlement publishes immediately. An opt-in browser stress test validates it.

reason: The Python SDK is in scope (DH-ADR-1), and testing the installed artifact with an identity check before any behaviour test is independent of what the runtime inside the wheel is written in.
summary: The Python SDK is tested as a user would install it: the built wheels are installed into a fresh virtual environment outside the repository, and the test first proves that the installed files, not the source checkout, are what runs.

reason: The goal, a deterministic whole-product regression suite that needs no API key, stands. Upstream's recordings are in its session format and cannot be used as they are (DH-ADR-2); the Go design records its own corpus in the Go format and keeps the method.
summary: One top-level corpus holds recorded sessions used as tests. Each scenario starts a shipped profile through the real launcher, replays the recorded model output, drives the product through a public interface, and requires the normalized saved session to equal the recording.

reason: Opening a session with more than a hundred thousand events is a user path the Go host must keep fast, and upstream learned it by regressing from 35 ms to 5 s. The budget values must be measured again for Go; the gate and its workload shape carry over.
summary: A required benchmark job fails a pull request when opening a very large session exceeds a time or memory budget. Benchmarks are grouped by the user path they measure and run compiled code in fresh processes.

reason: Request preparation that grows with history length is a risk in any implementation. The Go design should keep the three scenario groups and the synthetic history shape, with budgets measured for Go.
summary: Benchmarks measure the repeated cost of continuing a long, tool-heavy session: preparing each model request over a long history, running another tool-heavy turn, and discovering inactive fork children.

reason: The user paths stay and need budgets, but what is measured changes: there is no client-side fold or React paint. The Go benchmarks measure server render time, fragment size and browser responsiveness for the same workflow.
summary: Two browser-side budgets cover long sessions: reconnecting to an active stream, and one workflow that opens a long session cold, pages back, switches views and receives a paced reply while the user types.

reason: The goal, exercising the real update path without release infrastructure, stands. The mechanism is built on Electron's updater classes; the Go desktop shell (DH-ADR-3) has a different updater and needs its own loopback qualification.
summary: Desktop update downloads are qualified locally by running the real updater code against a loopback server that serves a test feed and inert bytes, with the installer call replaced by an observation, so no cloud storage or hardware signing is needed for a feedback cycle.

reason: An installed update ends the process that observed it in any desktop technology, so the evidence problem remains. The journal belongs to the Go desktop shell's updater (DH-ADR-3) and is redesigned with it; the whitelisting rule should be kept.
summary: When a qualification run sets a journal directory, each desktop process writes a small log of whitelisted update states and actions to it, so that evidence survives the installer replacing the application. Raw errors, addresses and chat content are never written.

reason: Isolation of test update material from real releases and user data is still required. The preparation steps operate on upstream's Electron runtime descriptor and inventory, which the Go desktop packaging (DH-ADR-3) does not have.
summary: The two versions needed for an installed-update walkthrough are prepared under a random test identity and a separate distribution namespace, with their own user-data directory, so that test builds can never be offered to real clients or touch real user data.

reason: Upstream test maintenance: a repair of two specific test files in its suite. The lesson (a test waits on the observed state, not on the clock) is a general habit for Go tests, not a design decision.
summary: Two flaky Windows test cases were changed to wait for the state they assert on instead of reading it after a fixed delay, and to print a timeline when they fail.

reason: Upstream test maintenance: a repair of two test files after a CI host leaked configuration. The lesson for Go tests that start Git is to build the child environment explicitly.
summary: Tests that start Git remove Git's command-line configuration variables from their environment first, so a CI host that exports them cannot change the result.

reason: Upstream test maintenance: a repair of one browser test of a third-party spreadsheet widget.
summary: A browser test of the spreadsheet preview selects a cell with the keyboard instead of a mouse click before resizing, because a click could be re-applied against a changed layout and select the wrong cell.

reason: Listing and search scale with the whole collection, and a uniform synthetic collection would understate the work. The measured size distribution is data the Go benchmarks can reuse directly.
summary: Benchmarks measure listing, content search and fork over a synthetic collection of sessions whose sizes follow the heavy-tailed distribution measured on a real user's 1,650 sessions.

reason: Behaviour on a small machine cannot be read from a 16 GB runner in any language. The Go runtime's garbage collector also reacts to a memory limit, so the rerun is as informative for Go as for Node.
summary: The heaviest benchmarks are run again inside a Linux control group limited to 4 or 8 GiB of memory with no swap; a case fails if it misses its normal budget or the kernel kills a process.

reason: The report is independent of what is measured and helps a reviewer judge a budget. It is a low-priority aid: the Go benchmark area may keep it as a small tool or defer it with a stated reason.
summary: Every benchmark run writes a self-contained HTML report that scales each measured time to older laptops and typical cloud machines and shows whether the working set fits in 4 or 8 GB, so a number can be read as user impact.

reason: Masking credentials in displayed user text stays a requirement, but it moves to the Go host that renders the HTML (DH-ADR-3). Inference: Go's standard `regexp` package guarantees linear-time matching, so most of the hand-built protection against backtracking is unnecessary; the list of credential formats and the performance gate are what carry over.
summary: Credentials in user text shown in the UI are found with a scan that is linear in the text length: one literal-only search finds where a known credential format starts, and only then is the format checked. Performance gates keep text without credentials nearly free and hostile input linear.

reason: Adopt the layering, not necessarily the build order. The two problems it solves, a model turn per poll and untrusted event text reaching the model as if the user wrote it, are independent of the language, and source providers fit compiled-in components or plugin processes. The schedule area should shape task storage so that time is one source among several, and may give the event sources a later priority.
summary: Proposal: an automation task becomes an instruction plus a source and a session mode, and time is only one source. A source provider (code, no model) reports changes; a shared trigger compares each observation with stored state and filters it, still without a model call; only a change that passes is delivered to a session, where the event content is quoted as data from the source and not as the user's words.

reason: Adopt the behaviour: fetch earlier history before the reader reaches the top, and never move what they are reading. The mechanism changes because the page is an HTML fragment fetched from the Go host (DH-ADR-3); a small script island must hold the fragment and insert it with the reading position preserved.
summary: Proposal: older chat history is fetched ahead of need but shown only at a safe moment. The client holds at most one fetched page, and the chat view decides when to insert it, so a page that arrives during a touch drag or an animation does not make the transcript jump.

reason: The Go design should not carry this over: it describes interactions between client-side session and chat classes that do not exist when the Go host renders the HTML (DH-ADR-3). The behaviour it implements is kept through the companion note on history prefetch.
summary: Proposal: the class-level design behind history prefetch, saying which client object owns the network request, which owns the decision to show the page, and how they call each other.

reason: TypeScript tooling: it proposes api-extractor or a declaration dump for npm packages, and was not built upstream. What a Go plugin author may rely on is the plugin protocol, which the stable API policy row covers.
summary: Proposal: generate a checked-in public API report per package so that every change to an exported type shows up as a diff a reviewer must see.

reason: Vendor drift disappears because the Go design builds on its own cordis port instead of vendored JavaScript source (DH-ADR-5). The other two parts still apply to Go modules: each module's version and licence is recorded and checked in a library row, and an advisory scan of the Go dependency list belongs to the toolchain decisions.
summary: Proposal: check nightly that the vendored framework equals its upstream at the recorded commit plus the logged local changes, scan the lock file for security advisories, and assert the licence inventory.

reason: TypeScript and npm tooling: the lists in question are `tsconfig` references and npm workspace inventories. Go discovers packages from the module itself.
summary: Proposal: derive package lists from the directory layout and manifests instead of maintaining static lists, in particular the TypeScript project references.

reason: Review practice of the upstream repository.
summary: Proposal: a private tool periodically scans merged pull requests for human review feedback and proposes updates to the code-review checklist used by coding agents.

reason: Repository mechanics: clean-up of a one-time migration script for upstream's test fixtures.
summary: Proposal: delete the temporary command that converted session test fixtures on in-flight branches to the current layout, once no open branch needs it.

reason: Upstream documentation process. The Go documents have their own writing rules in the research brief.
summary: Proposal: define "brief, intuitive and friendly" as reviewable outcomes for upstream's documentation, because the existing checks prove structure and freshness but not that the prose still names the live mechanism.

reason: Plugin authors need to know what they can rely on in the Go design too. What they rely on changes: an external plugin sees only the plugin protocol and MCP (DH-ADR-4), not in-process exports, so the stability promise attaches to protocol methods and events, each capability with its own version. Source markers and an export report are not the mechanism.
summary: Proposal: mark individual APIs as stable in source, version each capability seam on its own, generate one API report per release, and let CI fail when a stable entry changes incompatibly without a deprecation period and a major seam version.

reason: Adopt: the Go conversion queue should be built with resource limits only, and gain priorities when a real background consumer exists. Building the unused scheduling machinery again would repeat the debt the note identifies.
summary: Proposal: remove foreground and background priorities from the Office document conversion queue, because nothing in the product ever submits a background request; keep the queue's general resource limits.

reason: Adopt: this is where the Go design already stands. Go does not load code into a running process the way Node loads a module, so code replacement becomes a restart of the plugin process (DH-ADR-4), while watching and re-applying configuration remains a loader feature.
summary: Proposal: keep live refresh of profile configuration, and remove replacement of running JavaScript modules; a source or framework change requires a process restart.

reason: Adopt: one read path through the filesystem interface means instruction discovery works the same for local, sandboxed and SSH workspaces, and needs one set of error and cancellation tests.
summary: Proposal: instruction files (such as `AGENTS.md`) are found and read only through the filesystem provider; the second code path that reads the local disk directly, used only by tests, is removed.

reason: Adopt by omission: the Go model package should contain the first-token reader that session statistics and the trajectory view use, and not these five queries.
summary: Proposal: remove five exported helper functions that classify whether a streamed chunk is visible, because no product code calls them.

reason: Adopt: the SDK server never sends a request to the client, so the Go design's Python client can be one-directional from the start. The SDK wire protocol is free to change under DH-ADR-2, which makes this the cheapest moment to drop the unused direction.
summary: Proposal: the Python SDK client only sends requests and receives responses and notifications; its unused ability to receive requests from the server and answer them is removed.

reason: Adopt by omission: the Go boot package should expose one way to locate configuration and one way to load the environment, the ones the launcher uses.
summary: Proposal: remove two start-up helpers (an older configuration-path resolver and a single-file environment loader) that only test fixtures still call; the real launcher uses the layered environment loader and an absolute profile path.

reason: Adopt: the Go system-prompt registry should not publish a change event until a consumer needs one. An advertised event is a public promise with tests and ordering rules to maintain.
summary: Proposal: stop emitting an event when a system-prompt provider is registered or removed, because nothing in the product listens to it; the prompt is rebuilt for every model step anyway.

reason: Adopt: key ownership, conflict detection and refusal of undeclared output are the parts with consumers. The Go registry can start with a set of keys per contributor.
summary: Proposal: a plugin that contributes shell environment variables declares only the names it owns; the per-variable descriptions and the method that lists them are removed because nothing reads them.

reason: Adopt by omission: the Go query interface should offer the operations with real consumers (observations, batch titles, surface reads and traces) and add others on demand.
summary: Proposal: remove four convenience read methods and one result type from the session query service, because no product code calls them.

reason: Exists only because of JavaScript: the saving is one array copy and one `Object.freeze` traversal. Go has no freeze step; whether the classifier copies or borrows a slice is an implementation detail of that component.
summary: Proposal: the auto-review risk classifier stops copying and deep-freezing its input snapshot, because the only caller serializes it immediately.

reason: Adopt: decoding once at the wire boundary into a typed value is the ordinary Go shape, and the typed parameter states the precondition.
summary: Proposal: the SSH helper validates a sandbox policy once, when the request arrives, and passes the typed result on; the inner resolver no longer validates it a second time.

reason: Adopt: one canonical workspace path per call avoids repeated filesystem work and, more importantly, avoids two resolutions that could disagree if the path changes between them.
summary: Proposal: resolve the real path of a sandbox workspace once per confinement, in the code that derives the roots, instead of once in common preprocessing and again in each backend.

reason: Adopt all three. Replay equality is the core promise of an event-sourced session and is cheap to assert in every test, and Go's test runner already offers repetition, shuffling and a data-race detector for the stress run.
summary: Proposal: tests never sleep for a fixed time but wait for an event; after every agent-loop test the session log is replayed into a fresh session and must produce the same message history; and a nightly job repeats the loop and inbox tests many times in random order to expose races.

reason: Upstream test-process tooling: the proposal is to adopt a JavaScript tool (Stryker with the Vitest runner) and was not built upstream. Whether the Go project uses mutation testing is a quality-gate choice for the test strategy, not an upstream decision to account for.
summary: Proposal: run a mutation-testing tool that injects small bugs and checks that some test fails, as a counterweight to a line-coverage gate.

reason: The rejection still holds in Go. Knowing that a step finished without inferring it from neighbouring events is a property of the log, not of the language, and crash repair depends on it.
summary: Rejected proposal: remove the `step/start` and `step/end` events from the session log. Upstream keeps them, because `step/end` is the durable sign that a model request finished, and the pair makes crash repair, invariants and reading a transcript clearer.

reason: The goal of the rejection, a clean boundary between the session and its storage backends, still holds. The argument for a separate package does not transfer: upstream backends extend an abstract class and so must import the package that defines it, whereas a Go backend satisfies an interface without importing it. Package boundaries are free to change (DH-ADR-2), so the session area decides where the interface and the write coordinator live.
summary: Rejected proposal: move the storage contract and the shared write coordinator into the session package. Upstream keeps a separate contract package so that the boundary between session and storage backend stays clean.

reason: The rejection still holds in Go. One turn can contain many steps and large tool output, and silently dropping it after a crash loses real work; the Go session must define the same repair, including what the synthetic records say.
summary: Rejected proposal: on load, throw away everything after the last completed turn. Upstream instead keeps an interrupted final turn and closes it with synthetic records (error results for unanswered tool calls, a step end, and a turn end marked interrupted).

reason: The reason for the rejection still holds: a plugin must be able to contribute a skill while the host runs. The mechanism changes, because a third-party plugin is a separate process (DH-ADR-4); run-time skill registration has to be a call in the plugin protocol rather than a method on an in-process service.
summary: Rejected proposal: remove the method that lets a plugin register a skill directly at run time, because no shipped code calls it. Upstream keeps it as an intended extension path for third-party plugins.

reason: The rejection still holds in Go and costs less there: a small interface for compaction with the basic strategy as one implementation is ordinary Go, and the upstream tree already contains further compaction packages (image offload, tool-result pruning) beside the basic one.
summary: Rejected proposal: merge the compaction contract and its only complete backend into one package. Upstream keeps them apart because more compaction backends are planned.

reason: Exists only because of Node and Vitest: both the proposal and its rejection are about a Node built-in and a JavaScript test clock. A cancellable wait in Go is a `select` on a timer and the context.
summary: Rejected proposal: replace three hand-written cancellable sleeps with Node's built-in promise timers. Rejected because the test framework's fake clock does not intercept the built-in, so tests would become slow or non-deterministic.

reason: The named npm packages are irrelevant to Go, so the individual rejections do not transfer. The goal does: a recorded reason for each hand-written component. The Go design reaches it through library specifications (DH-ADR-5), and each "what the package cannot do" entry is a requirement the matching Go library choice must be checked against.
summary: Rejected proposal: more than thirty swaps of hand-written code for npm packages or Node built-ins. Each was rejected with evidence, and each entry names what the hand-written code does that the package cannot, such as a size bound on incoming messages, start-time identity for process trees, or wire faults in the mock model server.
